entries.title: axios (npm) Supply-Chain Compromise via Maintainer Account Takeover
entries.description: On 31 March 2026 an attacker took over the npm account of an axios maintainer and published malicious releases 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 of axios, one of the most-installed HTTP clients in the JavaScript ecosystem. The poisoned versions pulled in a malicious transitive dependency, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, that downloaded and executed a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT) with payloads for Windows, macOS and Linux during installation.
entries.impact: axios has over 70 million weekly npm downloads. Any project, CI/CD pipeline, or AI-agent-generated build that installed the malicious versions during the exposure window received a RAT capable of credential theft and persistent backdoor access.
entries.root_cause: Compromise (account takeover) of a package maintainer's npm account, allowing malicious versions of a trusted, widely-depended-on package to be published to the registry.
entries.notes: No CVE was assigned as of reporting. Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the associated infrastructure (including the plain-crypto-js account) to Sapphire Sleet, a North Korean state actor. The malicious versions were removed from npm and the attacker account was disabled.

entries.title: Moltbook: Production Database Exposed via Misconfigured Supabase (Vibe-Coded)
entries.description: Moltbook, an AI-agent social network launched on 28 January 2026, was built almost entirely from AI-generated ('vibe-coded') code. Wiz Research found a publishable Supabase API key embedded in the site's client-side JavaScript that granted unauthenticated read and write access to the entire production database, because Supabase Row Level Security was never enabled on the tables.
entries.impact: Wiz reported that the exposed database contained more than 1.5 million API authentication tokens, approximately 35,000 email addresses, private agent messages, and internal system metadata — all readable, and writable, without authentication.
entries.root_cause: AI-generated backend code shipped a Supabase key in client-side JavaScript and omitted Row Level Security, exposing the production database directly to any visitor.
entries.notes: Discovered by Wiz Research, which noticed the exposed key on 31 January and disclosed to Moltbook on 2 February 2026. Moltbook deployed fixes within hours of disclosure.

entries.title: Escape.tech Scan: ~2,000 Critical Vulnerabilities Across Vibe-Coded Apps
entries.description: Security firm Escape.tech passively scanned roughly 5,600 publicly deployed applications built on vibe-coding platforms including Lovable, Bolt.new and Base44. The study documents an insecure-by-default pattern in the output of these platforms: apps ship to production with exposed secrets, missing access controls, and leaked data.
entries.impact: Escape.tech reported more than 2,000 high-impact vulnerabilities, over 400 exposed secrets (API keys, credentials, tokens), and 175 instances of exposed PII — including medical records, bank/IBAN details, and phone numbers — across the scanned production apps. Escape describes the figures as a conservative, high-confidence lower bound.
entries.root_cause: Vibe-coding platforms generate and deploy full-stack applications without enforcing baseline security controls (secret management, authentication/authorization), and the resulting apps are frequently shipped without security review.
entries.notes: Aggregate research finding rather than a single-vendor disclosure. Published by Escape.tech in October 2025; date_disclosed is pinned to the month (day not stated in the sources reviewed).

entries.title: react-codeshift: Hallucinated npm Package Name (Slopsquatting Vector)
entries.description: AI coding tools repeatedly hallucinated an npm package named 'react-codeshift' — a plausible-sounding conflation of the real 'jscodeshift' and 'react-codemod' packages — that never actually existed. Aikido Security researcher Charlie Eriksen traced it to AI-generated agent skill files, and registered the unclaimed name defensively before a malicious actor could. Eriksen coined the term 'slopsquatting' for this attack class.
entries.impact: The hallucinated name propagated to roughly 237 repositories via forks and cloned agent skills and was still receiving daily install attempts from AI agents. Had an attacker registered the name first, any agent that auto-installed the hallucinated dependency would have executed attacker-controlled code. No malicious payload was ever published because the name was claimed defensively.
entries.root_cause: Slopsquatting: LLMs statistically hallucinate plausible-but-nonexistent package names, and AI coding agents install them without verifying that the package is real or trustworthy.
entries.notes: Registered defensively by a security researcher (Aikido); never weaponized. Included as a documented, real-world slopsquatting vector rather than a completed attack. Reported January 2026; date_disclosed pinned to the month (day not stated in the sources reviewed).
